1.title: a kitchen in amritsar feeds a hundred thousand a day
1.hook: a kitchen in Amritsar feeds a hundred thousand a day for free; the word for that
1.howItsDone: Sikhs do seva in the gurdwara by cooking and serving langar, cleaning, washing dishes and looking after shoes, and outside it through relief work and community service, usually as unpaid volunteers.

segments.voice: Picture a kitchen that never closes. In Amritsar, in northern India, next to the Golden Temple, there's a dining hall where anyone can walk in and eat. No ticket. No question about who you are or what you believe. On an ordinary day it serves tens of thousands of people, and on big days, a hundred thousand or more. Lentils, bread, rice, a sweet pudding. And here's the part that stops people: most of the hands doing the work are volunteers. A banker chopping onions. A teenager scrubbing steel plates. A grandmother rolling bread she'll never see eaten. Nobody's paid. Nobody's keeping score. There's a word for what those hands are doing, and it's your first word on this path.
screen: `A KITCHEN THAT NEVER CLOSES.` → `ANYONE CAN EAT.` → `NOBODY'S PAID.`

segments.voice: The word is seva. Selfless service. Work done for others with no reward in mind. It's a word Sikh children grow up hearing, and you'll see it everywhere once you know it: people cleaning the floors of a gurdwara, the Sikh house of worship, taking shoes at the door and handing them back polished, cooking, washing up, pouring water for strangers. Here's what makes seva different from being nice. It's done as part of the spiritual life, not beside it. In the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, the Gurus return to the idea again and again: service done with a humble heart is a way of drawing near to God. Not a warm-up for the real practice. The practice itself. Hands in the dishwater count. And seva has a condition that matters: it's meant to be done without ego. The hymns warn that service done to be seen, to be thanked or to be admired quietly turns into something else. That's why so much of it happens where nobody's watching. The person who scrubbed your plate at the Golden Temple doesn't know your name, and you'll never know theirs. That's not an accident. That's the point. Sikhs often describe three kinds of seva: with your body, like cooking or cleaning; with your mind, like teaching or listening; and with what you have, like giving money or food. So there's no one who can't do it. A kid can hand out water. Someone who can't stand for long can listen. And if you've seen Sikh volunteers turning up with hot meals after a flood or a fire, far from home, for people they'll never meet again, now you know the word they'd use for it.
screen: `SEVA — SELFLESS SERVICE.` · `NOT BESIDE THE PRACTICE. THE PRACTICE.` · `DONE WITHOUT EGO.` · `BODY, MIND, AND WHAT YOU HAVE.` · then, large: `HANDS IN THE DISHWATER COUNT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. Breathe in, and bring to mind one person who could use a hand today. Not a grand gesture. A dish, a text, a door held. Breathe out, and picture yourself doing it without telling anyone. That's all. One breath, one person, one quiet thing.
Seva. Selfless service, done for others with no reward in mind, and part of the spiritual life itself. First word.
Your line: one quiet thing for someone. Today, do one small act of service and don't mention it to anyone. Not online, not over dinner. Let it stay quiet. Day one.

2.title: wonder + teacher
2.hook: wonder + teacher; the word Sikhs say for God, and it means "wow"
2.tomorrow: a boy who wouldn't wear the thread
2.howItsDone: Sikhs repeat Waheguru in meditation, often slowly with the breath, say it in everyday moments of joy or difficulty, and greet each other with "Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh."

segments.voice: Yesterday: seva. Selfless service, done without anyone watching. Your line was one quiet thing for someone. Did you manage one, and did it stay quiet? Day two.

Think about the last time something actually took your breath away. Not impressive. Breathtaking. A night sky far from the city. The first time you held a newborn. The ocean after a long drive. What came out of your mouth? Probably not a sentence. Probably something like wow. A sound more than a word, the noise a person makes when the thing in front of them is bigger than their vocabulary. Now imagine a whole faith deciding that this sound, the wow, is the right way to speak about God. Today's word is the one Sikhs say for God, and at its heart is exactly that.
screen: `THE LAST TIME SOMETHING TOOK YOUR BREATH.` → `NOT A SENTENCE. A SOUND.` → `WOW.`

segments.voice: The word is Waheguru. Break it in two. Wahe: wow, wonderful, the cry of amazement. Guru: teacher, the one who leads from darkness into light. A popular explanation splits guru again, gu for darkness and ru for what removes it. Scholars debate that, but it's how many Sikhs hear the word. So Waheguru is something like: wonderful teacher. Or, closer to how it feels: wow, the teacher. Notice what kind of name that is. It isn't a title like king or judge. It's a reaction. Sikhs speak of a God with no form, no image, beyond description, and the scripture says again and again that no one can count or measure that greatness. So instead of a description, the name is a response. When words run out, you say wow. Waheguru is everywhere in Sikh life. It appears in the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, in hymns by the poets called the Bhatts. It's the word Sikhs repeat in meditation, slowly, on the breath. It's what someone says when they hear good news, or bad news, or when they stand up from the floor after sitting a long time. And it's in the greeting Sikhs trade with one another: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. The Khalsa, the community, belongs to Waheguru, and the victory belongs to Waheguru too. Ji, by the way, is a small word of respect, like saying sir or dear. So here's the idea to hold. On this path, wonder isn't a mood that happens to you once a year on vacation. It's a way of naming God, which means it's a way of paying attention. You can practice being amazed.

segments.voice: One breath, with the bell. Look at something near you, anything: your own hand, a window, a cup. Breathe in and really look at it, as if you'd never seen one before. On the way out, if you want to, let the word go with the breath, out loud or silently. Waheguru. Wow. That's the whole practice.
Waheguru. Wahe, wow. Guru, the teacher who leads into light. The word Sikhs say for God. Second word.
Your line: wow. Today, catch one ordinary thing that deserves it, a sky, a kindness, a good cup of tea, and let yourself actually say it. Day two.

3.title: a boy who wouldn't wear the thread
3.hook: a boy who wouldn't wear the thread; a man who walked for twenty years
3.carry: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim
3.tomorrow: the first symbol of the scripture
3.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Nanak as the first of ten Gurus and celebrate his birth each year with a festival, readings of the scripture and langar; his hymns open the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Waheguru. Wahe, wow. Guru, the teacher. Your line was just wow. What was the one thing that earned it? Day three.

A village in Punjab, more than five hundred years ago. The family has gathered, the priest has come, and there's food for the guests. It's a big day for a boy of about eleven: the ceremony where he'll receive a sacred thread, a cotton cord worn over the shoulder, a mark of his family's high place in the world. The priest sits him down and reaches for the thread. And the boy asks a question nobody expected. What is this thread for? And will it last? Everybody waits. Tradition says the boy politely refused to wear it. That boy grew up to be the first Guru of the Sikhs, and his name is today's word.
screen: `A FAMILY, A PRIEST, A SACRED THREAD.` → `WHAT IS THIS FOR?` → `THE BOY SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: Nanak. Guru Nanak, born in 1469 in a village called Talwandi, in what's now Pakistan. Everything on this path starts with him. Here's how the story of the thread goes on. Nanak wasn't being rude. He told the priest he'd gladly wear a thread, just a different one. In one of his own hymns, now in the Sikh scripture, he describes it: let compassion be the cotton, contentment the thread, self-control the knots, and truth the twist. A thread like that, he says, doesn't break, doesn't get dirty, doesn't burn, and isn't lost. That's Nanak in miniature. He didn't mock the ritual. He asked what it was pointing at, and then he went straight there. And then he walked. As a grown man, Nanak set out on long journeys, and tradition says they lasted over twenty years. On foot, across India and, the stories say, as far as Tibet, Sri Lanka, Mecca and Baghdad. His companion was a Muslim musician named Mardana, who played while Nanak sang. They visited Hindu holy places and Muslim ones, sat with yogis and Sufis and ordinary villagers, and kept asking the same kind of question he asked about the thread. What is this for? What's underneath it? Your line today comes from the moment his mission began. After an experience we'll come to later in the path, the first words he's remembered saying were: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. People have heard that in more than one way. Many Sikhs hear it as: beneath the labels, there are just people, all made by the one God. Others hear a challenge: nobody was truly living up to the name they carried. Both readings are told. And both sound like the boy with the thread.
screen: `GURU NANAK, BORN 1469.` · `COMPASSION FOR COTTON, TRUTH FOR THE TWIST.` · `TWENTY YEARS ON FOOT, WITH MARDANA.` · `THERE IS NO HINDU, THERE IS NO MUSLIM.` · then, large: `WHAT IS THIS FOR?`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. Think of one thing you do by habit: a ritual, a routine, something you've done so often you've stopped noticing. On the first breath, picture it. On the second, ask Nanak's question: what is this for? On the third, let the answer come, even if it's only half an answer.
Nanak. Guru Nanak, the first Guru of the Sikhs, born in 1469, who asked what things were for, and walked for twenty years. Third word.
Your line: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Today, when you meet someone, try seeing the person first and the label second. Day three.

4.title: the first symbol of the scripture
4.hook: the first symbol of the scripture — one
4.howItsDone: Ik Onkar opens the Guru Granth Sahib and begins the Mool Mantar, which Sikhs recite daily; the symbol is written, painted and worn as a reminder of the one God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nanak, the boy who asked what the thread was for. Your line was there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Did you catch yourself seeing a label before a person? Day four.

Open almost any book and the first thing you see is a title, or a name, or once upon a time. Open the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, fourteen hundred pages of hymns, and the very first thing on the very first page isn't a word at all. It's a symbol. You may have seen it without knowing: on a gold pendant, on a car's dashboard, painted over a shop door, tattooed on a forearm. It looks a little like the number one with a sweeping curve flying off it. Guru Nanak put it at the head of everything. Before any story, before any rule, before any song: this. Today, the first symbol.
screen: `FOURTEEN HUNDRED PAGES.` → `THE FIRST THING ISN'T A WORD.` → `IT'S A SYMBOL.`

segments.voice: It's called Ik Onkar. Look closely at how it's written. It starts with a numeral: the digit one. Not the word one. The number, the one you'd write on a price tag. That's Ik. Then comes Onkar, a very old sound for the divine, related to Om, the sacred syllable many of Nanak's neighbors already chanted. And then that curve, sweeping up and out, which many Sikhs read as a line with no end. Put it together and it says: there is one. One God, one reality, one source behind everything. So why a number instead of a word? Here's what Sikh teachers often point out. A word can be argued with. A word belongs to one language, one people. But a numeral is the plainest thing there is. Everyone agrees on one. Nanak seems to have chosen the least arguable mark possible to open his scripture. And notice what that one includes. On this path, the one God isn't somewhere far away looking down on creation. The hymns say the one is in everything, the whole of it: in you, in the person across the street, in the river and the dust. So if there's one, then nobody is outside it. You can hear yesterday's line underneath: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. If there's one, the labels come second. Ik Onkar is also a promise about the rest of the book. Everything that follows, all fourteen hundred pages, is an unfolding of this first mark. Tomorrow we'll read the line that comes right after it. Today, just the one.
screen: `IK — THE NUMERAL ONE.` · `ONKAR — AN ANCIENT SOUND FOR GOD.` · `A NUMBER NOBODY CAN ARGUE WITH.` · `IF THERE'S ONE, NO ONE IS OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `THERE IS ONE.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, notice yourself: your hands, your chest rising. On the second, notice something beyond you: a sound in the room, a person you love. On the third, hold both at once, and let the word ride out on the breath if you like: one.
Ik Onkar. The numeral one, with an ancient sound for God. There is one, and it opens the whole scripture. Fourth word.
Your line: one. Today, when someone annoys you, try thinking it just once: same source. See what it does. Day four.

5.title: "one creator, truth is the name"
5.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Mool Mantar at the start of the morning prayer Japji Sahib and at many other times; it stands at the head of the Guru Granth Sahib and is often the first passage children memorize.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ik Onkar, the numeral one that opens the scripture. Your line was one. Did it help, even once, with someone who annoyed you? Day five.

Most of us have a sentence we'd use to introduce ourselves. Name, where you're from, what you do. Now imagine being asked to describe God in a single breath. Not a book. Not a sermon. A few words, short enough to memorize as a child, deep enough to spend a lifetime on. Guru Nanak did exactly that. Right after the symbol for one, at the top of the scripture, comes a short statement Sikhs call the Mool Mantar, the root verse. Children learn it early. Many Sikhs say it every morning. It's only a handful of words in Punjabi, and it holds the whole path the way a seed holds a tree. Today, the first line.
screen: `DESCRIBE GOD IN ONE BREATH.` → `THE ROOT VERSE.` → `A SEED THAT HOLDS A TREE.`

segments.voice: Mool means root. Mantar is a sacred phrase, the Punjabi form of mantra. The root verse. It begins with yesterday's word, Ik Onkar, there is one, and then it says: Sat Naam. Karta Purakh. Take them one at a time. Sat means truth, but it's deeper than true as opposed to false. It comes from an old root meaning what really is, what exists, what lasts. Naam means name. So Sat Naam: truth is the name. Or, as some translate it, the one whose name is truth. The Victorian scholar Max Arthur Macauliffe, who spent years translating Sikh scripture with Sikh scholars beside him, put the opening this way: "There is but one God whose name is true, the Creator." Here's the surprise in naam. On this path the name isn't just a label, the way your name is printed on a bill. Naam comes to mean the whole presence of God, running through everything. So when Sikhs say they remember the name, they mean something like remembering what is real. Then: Karta Purakh. Karta, the doer, the maker. Purakh, the being, the person. The creator. Not a force that set the world going and walked away. The one who is still making. Put the line together and it holds three ideas in five words. There is one. Its name, its nature, is truth. And it creates. Nearly everything else in the scripture unfolds from this. And there's a quiet challenge in it. If truth is the name of God, then telling the truth isn't just manners. It's a way of speaking God's name.
screen: `MOOL MANTAR — THE ROOT VERSE.` · `SAT — WHAT REALLY IS.` · `NAAM — MORE THAN A LABEL.` · `KARTA PURAKH — THE ONE STILL MAKING.` · then, large: `THERE IS BUT ONE GOD WHOSE NAME IS TRUE.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, think of one true thing about your life right now, not the flattering version, just the true one. On the second, sit with it without fixing it. On the third, if you want to, let the words go out with the breath: Sat Naam.
The Mool Mantar, the root verse. Line one: Ik Onkar, Sat Naam, Karta Purakh. There is one, truth is the name, the creator. Fifth word.
Your line: the name is truth. Today, tell one small truth you'd normally smooth over, kindly. Day five.

6.title: "without fear, without hate"
6.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the whole Mool Mantar, including nirbhau and nirvair, at the start of Japji Sahib each morning, and the phrase is often held up as an ideal for how a Sikh should live.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mool Mantar, line one. Ik Onkar, Sat Naam, Karta Purakh. Your line was the name is truth. Which small truth did you tell? Day six.

Think about the last time you were really afraid of someone. A boss with your job in their hands. A bully. A voice on the phone. And now think about someone you've held a grudge against. Maybe for years. Fear and hate are strange twins. We fear the people who have power over us, and we resent the people we think have wronged us, and between the two they can take up a whole life. Five hundred years ago, in the root verse of the Sikh scripture, Guru Nanak described God with two words that cut right through both. Today, the second line of the Mool Mantar.
screen: `THE LAST TIME YOU WERE AFRAID.` → `THE GRUDGE YOU'VE KEPT.` → `TWO WORDS THAT CUT THROUGH BOTH.`

segments.voice: Nirbhau. Nirvair. Nir means without. Bhau means fear. Vair means enmity, hatred, the settled hostility of an enemy. So: without fear, without hate. Think about why those two belong together in a description of God. Fear is what you feel toward something that could hurt you. Hate is what you feel toward something you think is against you. A God who is one, who holds everything, has nothing outside to be afraid of, and no enemy to hate. The Victorian translator Macauliffe gave the phrase as devoid of fear and enmity. The root verse doesn't stop there. It goes on: Akaal Moorat, a form beyond time. Ajooni, never born. Saibhang, existing by itself. And it ends: Gur Prasad, known by the Guru's grace. But these two words, nirbhau and nirvair, have a special life of their own in Sikh memory, because Sikhs don't only say them about God. They take them as a picture of who a person can become. The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, wrote a short verse, now near the end of the scripture, describing the wise person as one who frightens no one, and is frightened by no one. Both halves matter. Being fearless isn't enough if it makes you frightening. Being gentle isn't enough if it makes you afraid. And Sikh history is full of people remembered for exactly this pair: standing up to the powerful without fear, and still refusing to hate. So nirbhau, nirvair isn't a description you admire from a distance. It's a direction. Less fear. Less hate. Both at once.

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, bring to mind one thing you're afraid of. Just name it. On the second, bring to mind one person you hold something against. On the third, loosen your grip on both, only a little, and let the words go out with the breath if you want: nirbhau, nirvair.
The Mool Mantar, line two. Nirbhau, nirvair: without fear, without hate. Said of God, and taken as a direction for a life. Sixth word.
Your line: nirbhau, nirvair. Today, in one conversation that makes you tense, try standing your ground without fear, and without making anyone an enemy. Day six.

7.title: remembrance
7.hook: remembrance; the name on the breath
7.tomorrow: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal
7.howItsDone: Sikhs practice simran by repeating Waheguru, silently or aloud, often in the early morning, sometimes with prayer beads, and also by singing the scripture together in the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mool Mantar, line two. Nirbhau, nirvair. Without fear, without hate. Did one tense conversation go a little differently? Day seven, the end of your first week.

You walk into a room and forget why you came in. You set your keys down and two minutes later they're gone. You meet someone at a party and their name falls out of your head before they've finished saying it. We forget all day long. Mostly it's harmless. But there's a deeper kind of forgetting too: whole days when you never once remember what matters to you, what you're grateful for, what you believe is real. You just get carried along. Sikhs have a word for the opposite of that, and a surprisingly physical way of doing it. Today, the word that ties this first week together.
screen: `WHY DID I COME IN HERE?` → `WHOLE DAYS OF FORGETTING.` → `THE OPPOSITE HAS A WORD.`

segments.voice: The word is simran. Remembrance. It comes from an old root meaning to remember, to call to mind. In Sikh practice it means remembering God, and especially remembering the name, the naam you met on day five, the whole presence of what is real. How do you remember something all day long? You tie it to something you do all day long anyway. You breathe. So one of the simplest forms of simran is this: breathe in with Wahe, breathe out with guru. The word from day two, riding on the breath. Some Sikhs do it sitting still in the early morning, some with a string of prayer beads, some while they drive, cook or fall asleep. It can be sung aloud with a whole room, or said silently, with no one around you any the wiser. The fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, wrote a long hymn called Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, and it keeps circling back to simran: remember, and remember, and remember, and find peace; remembering the name, he says, pain and worry fall away. And notice how this first week fits together. Seva, serving with your hands. Waheguru, the name that is a cry of wonder. Nanak, who kept asking what things were for. Ik Onkar, there is one. The root verse: truth is the name, without fear, without hate. Simran is how all of that stays with you after the lesson ends. Not by thinking harder. By remembering, gently, again and again, on the breath.
screen: `SIMRAN — REMEMBRANCE.` · `WAHE IN. GURU OUT.` · `REMEMBER, AND FIND PEACE.` · `HOW THE WEEK STAYS WITH YOU.` · then, large: `THE NAME ON THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. If you'd like to try simran the way many Sikhs do: breathe in slowly and let the word Wahe ride in with it. Breathe out and let guru ride out. Three times. If that word isn't yours, just remember one thing on each inhale that you don't want to forget today.
Simran. Remembrance: calling God, the name, to mind, again and again, often on the breath. Seventh word. One week.
Your line: remember on the inhale. Today, three times, at a red light, a kettle, a doorway, take one breath and remember. Next week: the kitchen, the work, the sharing. Day seven.

screen: `DAY 7 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERYONE ON THE FLOOR, EVERYONE THE SAME MEAL.`
